items.title: docs: realign the public documentation with v0.12.0
items.body:
The documentation was last realigned on 2026-07-08 against v0.10.0. Two releases shipped since. This brings all 45 site pages, the README, the roadmap and the example notes back in line with the code, and adds the one user-facing page that was missing entirely.

## What was wrong

An inventory of the public surface between that realignment and v0.12.0 found 147 changed or new symbols, 125 of them reachable by a user, including **eight breaking changes — none of which was marked as breaking anywhere**. A reader upgrading from v0.10.0 had no way to learn what would break.

An audit of 47 pages against `docs/DOCS-PROTOCOL.md` produced 95 findings, 56 of them red. All are addressed.

**Three documented examples could not run as printed.** `neural/rule-learning` called `program.query()` twice and built its entire "how you know it worked" section on the result; no such method exists on `CompiledProgram`, in the stub or in the bindings. `neural/exact-induction` printed `cand.left_rel_idx`, where `ScoredCandidate` carries relation *names*, so the example raised `AttributeError`. `probabilistic/engines` told readers to evaluate a probabilistic program with `xlog run`, which routes to the deterministic executor.

**A 28 KB page was unreachable.** `architecture/dilp-training` was listed in the navigation and simultaneously shadowed by a redirect sending its URL elsewhere. `mint validate` and `mint broken-links` both pass on that, which is why it had gone unnoticed; it was the only such page among 63 nav entries and 23 redirects.

**Two example READMEs described software that does not exist.** The supply-chain showcase documented a supplier/order/customer domain with a sample-output table; the actual example is warehouses, carriers and shipping lanes. The game-analytics one declared a predicate with the wrong arity and showed a fabricated rule.

**The Event-Calculus induction track had no user-facing page at all** — three merged pull requests, reachable only by reading source. That is R6 and R8 under the protocol.

## What changed

`neural/event-calculus-induction` is new: the feature's first user documentation, written to the protocol's page anatomy. Every command was validated by running it through its real argument parser, including the parse-time flag scoping that rejects `--max-body-literals 3` outside `--mode relational --protocol ec`. Every number is read from a committed result file. Abstention is in the lead rather than the footnotes, and the negative result is reported as one.

The reference pages now cover the v0.11–v0.12 surface: `log_z_e`, `prob_var_map`, `JointConstraintCarrier` and its two exceptions, `network_metadata`, the typed `register_network` parameters, `train_phi_gradient`, `--wcoj` — which `DOCS-PROTOCOL`'s own worked example told readers to type while the CLI reference did not list it — and all eight breaking changes, marked as breaking. `errors.mdx` gains `E0403`, which its table skipped, and all 17 distinct epistemic rejections where it previously had one generic row.

`examples/caviar_woled/` gains the README it was the only example directory to lack.

## Verification

`mint validate` and `mint broken-links` pass, matching the pre-work baseline. The doc-contract tests pass (19). Navigation resolves: 46 entries, 46 pages, no orphans, no shadowing, no dangling redirects.

Every changed factual claim traces to a `path:line` in the source. Claims that could not be traced were removed rather than softened.

## Note on one class of change

Benchmark figures were briefly withdrawn from this branch on the grounds that no committed artifact backed them, then restored. The reasoning was wrong: this repository's committed benchmark artifacts date from a February v0.4.0-alpha campaign, and a re-measurement on current code confirmed the published figures rather than the stale artifacts. The page now says which row's data can be opened and recomputed, and gives the procedure for measuring the others.

Independent of the paper and test branches open alongside it — the three touch disjoint paths and can merge in any order.

items.title: docs: correct drift between documentation and implementation
items.body:
> **Stacked on #81.** Base is `fix/disputes-schema-remnants` because that PR also touches `AGENT_PROMPTS.md`. GitHub will retarget this to `main` automatically once #81 merges.

## Context

Audited all nine docs plus the README against the code they describe. The drift was substantial, and concentrated in exactly the documents someone would open to check a claim.

Three findings would have caused real problems:

| | |
|---|---|
| `AGENT_PROMPTS.md` mandated **a model this project has never used** | `claude-haiku-3-5-20241022`, under the heading *"Always use this exact string"* — repeated in `ARCHITECTURE.md` and `DATABASE.md`, while README said the opposite |
| `DATABASE.md` produced **a database the app cannot run against** | Wrong env var names, wrong exported client function, no `model_type` / `is_synthetic`, neither benchmark function |
| `README.md` linked to **`docs/PRD.md`, which does not exist** | Four other docs cited it as their source of truth |

Every fix was verified against source. Nothing was inferred.

## Logic

**Prompts now match byte for byte.** The doc claimed to contain "the exact prompt templates"; all eight had diverged. The pillar agents' output blocks were missing 200/500-character caps, and the judge's was missing its concision instruction and per-field caps. I verified by extracting each fenced block and diffing it against the string literal in `src/lib/agents/` — 8/8 identical.

**The implementation snippet would have broken a reimplementation.** It wrapped the document in `<document>` tags before substitution, but the tags are already in the template — following it nests them. It also used `.replace()`, which substitutes only the **first** occurrence and interprets `$&`/`$1` sequences in the replacement string. Document text is untrusted input, so that is both incomplete and unsafe. The code uses `split().join()`; the doc now matches and says why.

**`SCHEMAS.md` no longer claims to be a complete transcription of `schemas.ts`** — that claim is precisely what let it drift, and it was missing eight exports while referencing identifiers it never defined. It is now framed as a reference that defers to the code.

**Two rule-vs-code conflicts documented rather than silently "fixed":**
- `confidence_label` bands in `AGENT_ARCHITECTURE.md` are now described as prompt convention, not an invariant — nothing derives the label from the numeric confidence.
- `AUTH_INVALID` is marked defined-but-unused; every route returns `AUTH_REQUIRED`.

## Edge Cases

- **`Promise.all` → `Promise.allSettled`** in three places. Not pedantic — `allSettled` is *why* the orchestrator can classify partial failures and retry only on `AgentParseError`/`AgentSchemaError`. Stating `Promise.all` describes a system that doesn't exist.
- **`REVOKE` is the privacy boundary.** `DATABASE.md` §2.6 now warns that recreating either `SECURITY DEFINER` function by hand without `REVOKE ... FROM PUBLIC, anon` silently opens cross-user aggregate access.
- **Rate limiting has no table** — `checkRateLimit` counts `submissions` rows via the service client, so `idx_submissions_user_id_created_at` is the covering index for that path, not just dashboard listing. Dropping it would degrade every submission.
- **I corrected two of my own claims mid-pass** rather than shipping them: I nearly wrote that the model string is centralised in `client.ts` (it is not — see below), and I cited a CSS token `--color-critical-border` that doesn't exist.

## Alternatives Considered

- **Rewrite `SCHEMAS.md` as a pure export table** — rejected as too large a change for this PR; reframing the claim plus fixing content removes the drift without discarding useful annotation.
- **Fix the model string in code instead of docs** — not applicable; the code was right and the docs wrong.
- **Delete `AUTH_INVALID`** — rejected; it's a reasonable future distinction, so documenting it as unused is more honest than removing it.
- **Delete the four "Extracted from PRD Section N" headers** — done, since the PRD is gone; replaced with self-describing one-liners rather than leaving dangling citations.

## Review Focus

**A finding I did not fix — it needs your call.** `src/lib/anthropic/CLAUDE.md` requires the model string to be *"defined once here, imported by agents"* and says *"Do not hardcode the model string in any other file."* It is hardcoded in **five**: all four agent modules plus `MODEL_USED` in `compliance/route.ts`. `client.ts` exports only `getAnthropicClient()` and no model constant.

Five copies is how the docs came to reference a model this project never used. I documented it as known drift in `AGENT_PROMPTS.md` rather than changing code in a docs PR. Worth a follow-up.

Also worth reviewing: `src/lib/security/validateMagicBytes.test.ts` tests `validateFileMagicBytes`, which lives in `sanitize.ts` — there is no `validateMagicBytes.ts`. The filename misleads.

---

| Field | Details |
|-------|---------|
| AI-generated | ~95% |
| Tool used | Claude Code (claude-opus-5) |
| Human review | Every claim checked against source before editing; two incorrect drafts caught and corrected during the pass. |

- [x] `npm run build` passes

- Every identifier named in `SCHEMAS.md` is exported by `schemas.ts`; every exported schema/enum is named
- Error codes 15/15, no set difference, no status mismatches

items.body:
There was no site. `docs/` held three bare markdown files with no Jekyll config, no theme, and no Pages setup, so nothing was ever hosted.

The content had also drifted badly — `API.md` and `SPDX.md` were last touched at v1.5.6, `USAGE.md` at v1.6.0, against a current release of 1.7.1.

## What was actually wrong

| Gap | Detail |
|---|---|
| Undocumented CLI flags | `--fast`, `--detail`/`--evidence-detail`, `--max-file-size`, `--skip-content-detection`, `--skip-extensionless`, `--skip-smart-read` |
| Documented but never existed | `--cache-dir` |
| Third-party category (1.7.0 headline) | `get_own_licenses()` / `get_third_party_licenses()` appeared in **zero** files |
| Undocumented `Config` fields | 7 of 18 |
| Detection methods | `keyword` missing from the documented list |
| Dead link | README linked to `docs/BENCHMARK_SCANCODE.md`, removed in #56 |
| Wrong requirement | README claimed Python 3.8; the floor is 3.9 |

## The site

Follows the layout upmex already uses: just-the-docs as a remote theme, pretty permalinks, search, and an edit link back to each page's source. Pages renamed to lowercase so published URLs read `/usage/` rather than `/USAGE.html`.

Six pages, up from three:

| Page | Status |
|---|---|
| Overview | new — what osslili is, installing, first run |
| Usage | rewritten — every flag, grouped by what it affects; modes explained by which files each reads |
| Detection | **new** — tier cascade, methods, categories, confidence, and what osslili refuses to report |
| Python API | rewritten against the real signatures |
| Configuration | **new** — schema split out of the API reference, every field with its default |
| SPDX data | rewritten — refreshing the bundled list |

Detection covers what previously had no home, including why the fuzzy tier corroborates its own candidates and why an unversioned GPL mention yields nothing — the behaviour introduced in #92.

## Package metadata

`Documentation` now points at the published site instead of GitHub-rendered markdown. Verified in a built wheel:

```
Project-URL: Documentation, https://semclone.github.io/osslili/
```

This reaches PyPI on the next release — 1.7.1 already shipped before this change existed.

## Verification

Every documented default was checked against the code rather than carried over. That surfaced a genuine inconsistency: `--max-extraction-depth` defaults to `10` and always sets the value, while a bare `Config` defaults to `3`, so CLI and library disagree. Both are documented where they apply, with a note on the mismatch.

Front matter, nav ordering, and every internal and README link are checked by a validation pass. Tests remain at 127 passing.

**A full Jekyll build was not run locally** — the system Ruby is 2.6, too old for the `github-pages` gem. The first real build will be the one Pages performs, so the build is worth watching once Pages is enabled.

## To enable

Settings → Pages → Source: *Deploy from a branch* → `main` / `/docs`. The configured URL is `https://semclone.github.io/osslili/`.

items.title: Add Round 5 consultation analysis: architecture strategy verification
items.body:
## Summary

Add comprehensive Round 5 consultation document (`207_OPUS_ROUND5_ANSWER.md`) that verifies the architecture strategy outlined in documents 202–206 against the actual committed code, hand-checked arithmetic, and primary literature sources.

## Key Findings

This analysis document establishes that:

1. **Repository state mismatch**: Five claimed implementations from document 206 are not present in the committed code:
   - PSRHead remains at 70.9M parameters (6 layers, d=768, ff=8×), not the claimed 1.78M diet
   - ActivityHead instantiated without `logit_adjust` flag despite claims of enablement
   - No `--kendall-uncapped` flag exists in code (only in documentation)
   - `scripts/overfit_probe.py` does not exist
   - No run12 artifacts (logs, checkpoints, eval JSON) in repository

2. **Technical errors in strategy documents**:
   - VideoMAE ViT-B benchmark number is wrong (87.4% claimed vs ~81.5% published), invalidating Lever 1
   - Per-task LoRA adapters on backbone Q/V require four forward passes, contradicting the single-forward-pass efficiency claim
   - Detection-conditioned PSR head spec contains a confirmed bug: mean-pool-then-expand produces identical logits for all 8 frames, making per-frame transition localization impossible
   - Nash-MTL pseudocode in 204 does not match published algorithm (Gα=1 vs GᵀGα=1/α)

3. **Code/documentation drift**:
   - Kendall loss caps in code (det:4.0, pose:4.0) differ from documented values (det:1.5, pose:2.0)
   - Detection has weakest starvation protection (exp(-4)≈0.018 weight floor)
   - Logit-adjust applied unconditionally at eval, self-canceling the debiasing effect

4. **Validated claims**:
   - PSR diet arithmetic is correct (1.78M at d=256/2L/ff=1024)
   - 6D rotation + geodesic loss is the correct SO(3) approach
   - Decoupled training and logit adjustment are principled long-tail fixes
   - Detection augmentation (mosaic/copy-paste) has strong published evidence

## Recommendations

**Immediate actions** (before any architecture changes):
- Push actual run12 code state and result artifacts
- Run overfit probe on all four heads (pending for five rounds)
- Launch ST baselines (pose, activity, detection)
- Wire and run `--kendall-uncapped` ablation

**Architecture decisions**:
- **Accept**: Detection neck (BiFPN@128) — but gate behind probe + augmentation
- **Reject**: VideoMAE swap (wrong benchmark), per-task backbone LoRA (breaks latency claim), Nash-MTL swap (deletes methodological contribution)
- **Defer**: Detection-conditioned PSR (spec bug + depends on 0.000-mAP detector), SlowFast rewrite (−4.86 top-1 vs SOTA anchor)

**Paper spine** (unchanged, round 5):
Kendall-collapse characterization + fix (methodological contribution) + measured MTL/ST transfer map + genuine ~2× parameter efficiency at single-pass latency.

## Authority Rule

Where this analysis and documents 202–206 disagree, the committed code, hand-checked arithmetic, and primary sources are authoritative. This establishes a standing requirement: no consultation round N+1 opens until round N's code diff and ≥1 result artifact are pushed to the repository.

items.body:
# RX72N TSIP fixes and command-line build/flash/UART tooling

## TSIP crypto/hardware fixes

- **`tsip_ImportPublicKey` / `wc_tsip_generateSessionKey`**: fixed `tsip_hw_lock()` leaks on allocation failure (`renesas_tsip_util.c`) — an `XMALLOC` failure returned early without calling `tsip_hw_unlock()`, permanently holding the TSIP hardware lock. (f5419)
- **`TSIPHashFinal` / `TSIPHashGet`**: fixed silent-success-on-failure bugs in `renesas_tsip_sha.c` — `ret` was left uninitialized on some paths, a `Final()` call that succeeded with the wrong output size still returned `0` (success), and `TSIPHashGet` unconditionally `return 0` regardless of the actual result. (f6162)
- **`wc_tsip_AesGcmDecrypt`**: fixed a copy-paste bug where the 32-bit-aligned `aadBuf` was allocated and filled but never used — the TSIP `updateFn` call passed the original (possibly unaligned) `authIn` pointer instead, unlike the correct encrypt-side code. Could cause `AES_GCM_AUTH_E` on valid input when the caller's AAD buffer isn't aligned. (f6163)
- **`tsip_Tls13AesEncrypt`**: fixed two error-log messages copy-pasted from the decrypt function (said "Decrypt" instead of "Encrypt"); no functional impact, diagnostics only. (f1535)

## build.bat, debug_run.bat, and UART output

- Routed `printf()` to the on-board SCI2 UART (switchable back to the E1/E2 Virtual Console via `BSP_CFG_USER_CHARPUT_ENABLED`), and fixed the underlying clock-forcing and baud-rate calculation bugs that caused wrong benchmark timing and garbled UART output.
- Rewrote `debug_run.bat` to flash and run via Renesas Flash Programmer instead of a raw GDB session (more reliable — sidesteps device-specific GDB setup e2studio's GUI does internally).
- `build.bat` now accepts `crypt`/`bench`/`TLSClient` to switch the demo mode before building, fixes a stale-object incremental-build bug, and fails with a clear message on a not-yet-bootstrapped checkout.
- Updated README_EN.md / README_JP.md accordingly.

items.title: fix: correct tier-2/3 CER (<DR> editor-token contamination) + v0.1.1 corrections
items.body:
## The public benchmark ships wrong numbers

`benchmark-v0.1.0` reports tier-2 CER **0.0172** and tier-3 **0.0234**. Both are wrong.

| figure | v0.1.0 (withdrawn) | corrected |
|---|---|---|
| tier-2 CER, B vs consensus | 0.0172 [0.0105, 0.0248] | **0.0031 [0.0006, 0.0062]** |
| tier-3 CER, B vs consensus | 0.0234 [0.0166, 0.0309] | **0.0119 [0.0085, 0.0156]** |
| adjudication, tier-2 edits | 165 | **33** |
| adjudication, tier-3 edits | 280 | **148** |

## Cause

`<DR>`, the annotator-tool token for a double *rafe*, was scored as four literal ASCII characters in the tier-2/3 CER path. `iaa/cer.py` asserted editor tokens were "already stripped during `split_chunks`" — they were not. `split_chunks` strips only `PASSTHRU_TAGS`, and `<DR>` is deliberately excluded so tier-4 extraction can emit a `double_rafe` record from it. Nothing removed it afterwards.

The three sides carry unequal counts (A 25, B 56, consensus 27), so every excess token scored as four spurious edits.

Self-contradictory as well as wrong: `strip.py` already excludes U+05BF (*rafe*) from tier 2 precisely "so it is not double-counted across tiers". The single *rafe* was stripped; the double *rafe*, in ASCII, was not.

## Direction

**Conservative.** The bug made the two annotators look *less* consistent than they are. No conclusion reverses.

## Not affected

Verified field-by-field over regenerated result JSONs — **262 tier-4 and stratification fields compared, zero changed**: tier-1 CER 0.0029; tier-4 F1 exact 0.9187; Krippendorff α 0.7470; BL-05 *rafe* baseline F1 0.6210; every corpus count. Tier 1 is immune because its projection keeps only Hebrew consonants, space and *maqaf*.

## Also in this PR

- **`personnel_note` removed** from four public fixtures — it named a collaborator in full alongside an internal personnel correction and referenced a private-repo file. It remains in the immutable `v0.1.0` tag.
- **David Zev Moster added** to `CITATION.cff`, README citation, `LICENSE.md` attribution and `ACKNOWLEDGMENTS.md`. He produced half the reported agreement and was named only in the changelog and data files, while his projection ships under attribution-required terms.
- **Two false statements removed from this repo's own documentation.** `generate_iaa_report.py` claimed in two places that the headline CER was "NOT recomputable without the gitignored UXLC 2.5 cache." Tiers 1–3 recompute from the three committed projections alone. **Two independent external reviewers repeated that claim in their audits, having taken it from this docstring rather than testing it.**
- The shipped `_note` described the metric as code-point Levenshtein on NFC; it is cluster-aligned code-point CER on NFD, macro-averaged over verses.

## Structural fix

`masoretic_eval.iaa.cer.tier_view()` is now the single definition of a chunk's scoring view. The same sequence had been inlined in **three** places — `cer.py`, `scripts/generate_iaa_report.py`, and the release test meant to guard reproducibility — and the latter two would have silently missed the new strip.

Regression test `tests/iaa/test_editor_token_cer_isolation.py` asserts tier CER is invariant to editor tokens at every tier, and that tier-4 extraction still consumes `<DR>`.

## Gates

- `pytest` — 360 passed, 8 skipped
- `generate_iaa_report.py --check` — ok
- `verify_gt_hash.py --check` — ok
- `audit_release.py --all --release-tier` — **PASS**

## Provenance

Found while verifying three independent external reviews of `benchmark-v0.1.0`. The tier-3 half was flagged by the Codex reviewer; the larger tier-2 half and the adjudication-count contamination were found during verification of that finding.

items.title: command3: test the benchmark suite directly and document what it proves
items.body:
## The gap

`modelBenchmarks.ts` had **no direct tests**. `benchmarkLedger.test.ts` reaches it only through aggregation, so a definition could lose its `successCriterion`, or `sampleBenchmarks` could start returning the whole suite, without anything failing.

Both are failures that surface as provider spend rather than a red build — the wrong place to find them.

## Tests added (17)

`backend/src/ai/modelBenchmarks.test.ts`, covering the parts that cost money when wrong:

- Every benchmark states how it is settled without asking a model (`objective`, `successCriterion`, `evidenceKind` all non-empty).
- Benchmark ids are unique — duplicates would silently merge two measurements into one ledger entry.
- Sampling is capped at 8 and never returns the whole suite; §21 forbids running it all on a user request.
- Heavy benchmarks are dropped first, so measurement cost stays below the cost of the work being measured.
- A narrow filter yields the heavy benchmark rather than silence — returning nothing would read as "unmeasurable" when it is only expensive.
- A language filter does not exclude `language: null` benchmarks, which would drop review, debugging and refactor coverage the moment a language was named.
- A failed result never records under the evidence kind a success would have produced (`tests_passed` → `tests_failed`, `patch_applied` → `patch_rejected`, `repair_succeeded` → `repair_failed`).
- An empty history summarises to `null`, not `0` — "never measured" and "0% pass rate" are different claims.
- Median latency is the middle, not the mean.

## Documentation

Three new documents, each covering ground no existing document did:

| Document | Covers |
| --- | --- |
| `docs/model-evaluation-system.md` | The suite, the ledger seam, the eight maturity gates, and how measured evidence reaches `chooseCostAware` |
| `docs/learning-data-governance.md` | The five learning-data kinds, the eight capture conditions, and why fine-tuning consent is not implied by data-use permission |
| `docs/migration-and-rollback.md` | The three conditions a migration slice must meet, what has landed, what has not, and how each step is undone |

The evaluation doc states plainly that **no runner executes the suite against live providers**. The definitions, scoring shape, aggregation and routing consumption all exist and are tested; the component that spends provider budget to populate them does not. A suite that looks complete and has never run is the most misleading artifact in an evaluation system, so it is named rather than left to be discovered.

## Stale-claim correction

`docs/universal-agent-rollout.md` said:

> The *enabled* path is not yet wired: no real build routes through `planUniversalRun` to generate files, so setting `enabled` today changes only the routing decision.

That has been false since `pipeline.ts` began routing through `atomicGitHubCommit` (`pipeline.ts:1168`, `:1214`). A document asserting the opposite of current behaviour is worse than no document. The replacement states what is actually wired, and that no live run has yet produced a commit — the `liveRunProducedCommit` condition tracked in `execution-state.json`.

## Verification

Full backend suite: **1610 pass / 0 fail** (up from 1593). `npx tsc --noEmit` clean.

items.title: docs: audit documentation against the engine; fix false claims and two code bugs
items.body:
## Why

A five-way parallel audit of this package's documentation against ferx-core `aa70743d`, covering
fit options, the exported API, prose claims, examples/bundled assets, and long-form docs.

The useful result is *where* the rot was. **Everything mechanical is clean**: `R CMD check`'s
documentation checks pass (`checkDocFiles`, `undoc`, `checkRdContents`, `checkS3methods` all
empty), `man/` regenerates byte-identically, the `ferx_example()` registry has zero broken
entries, `_pkgdown.yml` resolves completely, and no vignette chunk would error. Every real defect
was **semantic** — a statement or a fixture that no tool can check. Two turned out to be code
bugs rather than documentation at all.

#281 is merged, so this targets `main` and stands alone.

## What changed

### Code, not docs

- **`ferx_example("warfarin_scaled")` could not be fitted.** `inst/examples/models/warfarin_scaled.ferx:42`
  shipped `gradient = ad`. The Enzyme path was retired in favour of the analytic `Dual2`
  sensitivities, so the engine now rejects that token outright (`E_AD_RETIRED`,
  `src/api/validation.rs:1864`), and `inst/examples/ex_warfarin_scaled.R:14` fits it with no
  override — so a documented public example died immediately. It was the only model carrying it.
  The vignette chunk that fits it survived only because it is `eval = FALSE`.
- **`fit$gradient_used` never reported the analytic gradient.** `.ferx_short_gradient_label()`
  still translated the dead `"Enzyme AD"` and had **no case** for the engine's actual
  `"analytic (Dual2)"` (`src/build_info.rs:48`), so the long string fell through unmapped:
  `fit$gradient_used == "ad"` was permanently `FALSE`, and `print()`/`summary()` rendered
  `toupper()` of the raw engine string.

### Actively harmful advice

- **The `[scaling]` help told users to disable their exact gradient.** Both the reference and
  `special-features.Rmd` said expression divisors (form B) and Form C readouts force
  finite differences, and to add `gradient = fd`. Both are differentiated **exactly** under the
  default `gradient = auto` (#486) — the engine says so in as many words at
  `src/estimation/inner_optimizer.rs:63-70`, which describes the FD route as *vestigial* Enzyme-era
  behaviour. Following the advice cost the analytic gradient **and** flipped `Optimizer::Auto`
  from L-BFGS to BOBYQA. Only the per-CMT variants fall back, and they do so **silently** — now
  stated, with a pointer to `fit$gradient_used`. The stated *reason* was also wrong: form B runs
  on the analytical closed-form path, not "through the ODE machinery".
- **`bloq_method = "drop"` was described as discarding BLOQ rows.** It keeps them and fits each at
  the limit value in `DV` as though measured there (`src/types.rs:5570`) — a materially biased
  analysis nobody would choose knowingly. The variant *name* is the trap; the docs repeated it
  instead of compensating. Now corrected, pointing at `ignore = "CENS == 1"`.

### Wrong facts

Each verified against engine **source**, not engine docs:

| Claim | Was | Actually |
|---|---|---|
| `inner_tol` | `1e-4` | `1e-5` (`types.rs:5449`) — and it changes the converged point |
| `n_mh_steps` | `10` | `20` (`:5487`) |
| `impmap_proposal_df` | `"normal"` (MVN), "the NONMEM default" | Student-t `4.0` (`:5518`); ferx diverges from NONMEM deliberately |
| `threads` | one worker per logical CPU | cores − 1, capped at 8 (`pool.rs:53,61`) |
| `max_unconverged_frac` | relaxes the converged flag | **rejects the outer step** (OFV = ∞) |
| `covariance_method` `s`/`rsr` | "rejected under non-interaction FOCE" | supported for FOCEI, FOCE and IOV |
| `optimizer = "bfgs"` | hand-rolled BFGS | deprecated alias for `nlopt_lbfgs`; the built-in is unreachable |
| `gradient = "ad"` | "accepted by older model files" | hard validation error |
| `method = "laplace"` | NONMEM `LAPLACIAN` | `LAPLACIAN INTER` — plain differs by ~9 OFV units |
| CV → omega approximation | "under-estimates" | over-estimates (since `log(1+x) < x`) |
| `analytic_cov_hessian` scope | excludes `laplace` | also excludes `focei` with `n_agq > 1` |

The `impmap_proposal_df` inversion is the one I'd flag hardest: a user reading `?ferx_fit`
concluded their IMPMAP run used a Gaussian proposal when it used t(4), and the engine chose the t
precisely *because* a Gaussian's lighter tails bias the M-step moments.

### Full fit-option coverage

`?ferx_fit` documented 56 of ~98 keys; the remainder were reachable through `settings` all along
(the R glue whitelists nothing — unknown-key rejection is the engine's) but findable only by
reading ferx-core source. **Now 99 of 101.** The two exceptions are `frem_predictions` and
`frem_sigma`, structural maps `ferx_model_to_frem()` writes for you; the help now says so, so the
omission reads as intentional rather than as the same gap.

Every default was re-derived from the engine's `Default` impl and parser rather than copied from
engine prose — which is exactly what caught the wrong ones in the first commit.

Two of the additions change the meaning of options that were *already* documented, and matter more
than the new entries:

- **`imp_auto` / `impmap_auto` default to `TRUE`**, so `imp_samples` / `impmap_samples` are
  *starting* counts that ramp (×2 per iteration, capped 10000) while the objective's Monte-Carlo SE
  exceeds 1.0 — not the fixed counts they were described as. The existing "quadruple the samples to
  halve the MC SE" guidance only holds with the adaptive mode off.
- **The applicability headings were understated.** `method = "laplace"` accepts the entire
  outer-optimizer block and `maxiter`, and the inner-loop keys are accepted by `"imp"`, `"impmap"`
  and `"bayes"` too — so a reader tuning Laplace had no documented way to set its iteration cap or
  optimizer at all.

Also records that `cov_inner_tol` may draw a spurious "not used by method … will be ignored"
warning even though the value *is* applied (the engine bug below), and corrects the reserved-key
list, which omitted `bloq`, `gradient` and `gradient_method`.

### Structure and fixtures

- **`Version:` → `0.2.0.9000`, new development NEWS heading.** `v0.2.0` is a real tag
  (`fe0179f`, 2026-07-03) and ~200 lines of post-release entries had been appended into that
  shipped section. The released content was **not contiguous** — entries were interleaved into
  existing subsections — so rather than guess, I classified each bullet against
  `git show v0.2.0:NEWS.md` and verified bullet counts identical before and after (149 → 149,
  zero lost, zero invented). *My own #281 entries were among the misfiled ones.*
- **`^vignettes/articles$` added to `.Rbuildignore`.** Only `model-workflow.Rmd` is a real
  vignette; R's scanner does not recurse, so the six files under `vignettes/articles/` were
  shipping in the tarball unindexed.
- `print.ferx_data` gains the `@return` it needed — the only non-internal page with `\usage` and
  no `\value`.
- Fixture corrections: a `max_iter` typo in `summary.ferx_fit`'s examples that would have thrown
  (the key is `maxiter`, and unknown settings keys are a hard error — it hid inside `\dontrun{}`);
  a dataset header naming the wrong file *and* the wrong subject count (claimed
  `warfarin.csv`/32 subjects, resolves to `warfarin_ode_lagtime.csv`/20 — both counts verified by
  reading the CSVs); a reference to a nonexistent `bioavailability_oral.csv`; a `v=` alias on a
  2-cpt model where every sibling writes `v1=`; and two example scripts naming `bobyqa`/`slsqp` as
  "the default" optimizer when the default is `auto`.
- Adds the missing NEWS entry for **ferx-core #899** (`CMT=0` on ODE datasets), which the engine
  changelog says changes predictions — earlier results need regenerating.

## Alternatives considered

**Trusting the workers' reports.** I verified each headline claim myself, which was justified:
two workers reached **opposite** conclusions on `covariance_method` (one said FOCE is supported,
the other listed FOCEI-only as *verified correct*). I settled it from source — there is no
validation gate tying it to `interaction` and no rejection diagnostic exists, so worker 1 was
right. Two of my own briefing premises were also wrong: `method = "agq"` and the Enzyme shim are
already documented correctly, and I had flagged both as suspects.

**Mechanically splitting NEWS by line diff.** Rejected once I confirmed the released content is
non-contiguous; a naive split would have fabricated release history.

## Breaking changes (R users)

- [x] **`fit$gradient_used` return value changes** — from an unmapped raw `"analytic (Dual2)"` to
      `"analytic"`. Any code testing `== "ad"` was already always `FALSE`, so nothing that
      *worked* breaks, but code matching the raw string will need updating.
- [ ] Function signature changed
- [ ] Output column names / types changed

No engine pin change in this PR, so no numerical results move.

## Tests

- [ ] `testthat` tests added / updated
- [ ] `R CMD check` passes
- [ ] Test against real ferx-core binary

**Not run locally, and cannot be** — this box has only the MSVC Rust toolchain and extendr needs
GNU. Static verification: `roxygen2::roxygenise()` regenerated exactly the three `.Rd` files
matching the three edited `R/` files with no churn, `tools::checkDocFiles()` is empty, and every
engine claim above was read out of ferx-core source. **CI is the first thing that compiles this**,
so please treat its result as the real check.

Worth adding and not done here: a test that `ferx_example("warfarin_scaled")` parses and fits, which
is what would have caught the `gradient = ad` breakage. The repo's stated policy is to run every
`ex_*.R` end-to-end; nothing enforces it, which is why a public example could sit broken.

## Docs

- [x] `roxygen2` docs regenerated
- [x] `NEWS.md` entry added
- [x] Vignettes corrected (`special-features.Rmd`, `parameter-transforms.Rmd`)

## Reviewer hints

Two commits (`cdefbc0`, `d2ff13d`). The `[scaling]` gradient rewrite and the `bloq_method = "drop"` rewrite are the two
worth reading closely — they change *advice*, not just facts. Everything in the wrong-facts table
is a one-line substitution you can check against the cited engine line.

The NEWS restructure is the only mechanically risky change; the bullet-count invariant is the
thing to check if you doubt it.

## Open questions — deliberately left out of scope

Ranked by what I'd do next:

1. **`transit_2cpt` fits the wrong model to its own data.** The registered model dropped
   `TVLAG`/`LAGTIME` (the orphan copy at `inst/examples/transit_2cpt/` still has them), but
   `simulate_dataset.R:7,48,58` generated the shipped CSV with `TVLAG <- 0.25` and lag-shifted
   observation times — so MTT silently absorbs a 15-minute lag. Needs a decision (restore the
   parameter, or regenerate the data with `TVLAG <- 0`), not a mechanical fix.
2. **Frozen vignette numbers are probably already stale.** `model-workflow.Rmd:250-257`
   (SE/RSE%/CI) and `uncertainty-sir.Rmd:100-117` (`sir_ess = 4.71` and all three CI matrices) are
   `eval = FALSE` blocks from a warfarin fit. Warfarin **is** in `analytic_cov_hessian` scope, and
   #953 changed those SEs — exactly what #281's own NEWS entry warns about. They cannot error,
   which is why they need explicit regeneration.
3. **`sir_ess` may be wrong by ~66×.** The engine benchmarks the same dataset at the same sample
   count and reports ESS 310 (`docs/estimation/sir.qmd:65-71`) against the vignette's 4.71 — and
   the vignette builds a whole "the warfarin asymptotic covariance does not faithfully represent
   the true uncertainty" narrative on that number. Needs one run to settle.
5. **No long-form doc covers time-to-event**, despite `survival` being a default feature,
   `ferx_predict_survival()` being exported, and five TTE models shipping. Highest-value new
   vignette. Also uncovered: estimation-method selection, and the post-fit diagnostics family
   (`ferx_xpose`, `ferx_calc_npde`, `check_diagnostics`, …) — 19 of 37 exports appear in no
   vignette or README.
6. **`print.ferx_fit` has no help page** (bare `@export`, no title), along with four other S3
   methods — it is the primary visible output of `ferx_fit()`.
7. **Dead weight**: 12 byte-identical duplicate CSVs that `.data_aliases` exists to prevent; an
   orphan `inst/examples/transit_2cpt/` directory; and a top-level `examples/` shadow copy
   (`.Rbuildignore`d) whose models carry an `[initial_values]` block the engine does not read at
   all — `extract_blocks` silently swallows unknown blocks, so a contributor copying from it gets
   silently ignored initial estimates.

### Two engine-side bugs, for ferx-core rather than here

- **`cov_inner_tol` emits a spurious "will be ignored" warning for an option that *is* applied.**
  It has a working `apply_fit_option` arm and a `fit-options.qmd` entry but appears in neither
  `framework_keys()` nor any `method_specific_keys()` arm, so `unsupported_keys_warnings` cannot
  find it. Same class as the `analytic_cov_hessian` gap #953 fixed; the guard test only checks
  advertised → arm, never the reverse.
- **`fit-options.qmd:38`** states the `global_maxeval` auto budget as `200 * (n_params + 1)`; the
  code uses `30 * (n + 1)` (`outer_optimizer.rs:899`). `200*(n+1)` is only what a source comment
  offers as a manual "thorough sweep".
- Also noted: the covariance non-PD wording is FD-specific in both repos, but the trigger is not —
  the non-PD branch runs on whichever R-matrix was assembled.

items.title: protocol(doc-gate): preflight checks the committed RANGE — --staged was vacuous
items.body:
Self-reported protocol violation from PR #80, and the gate change that prevents it recurring.

## What went wrong

PR #80 (Vulkan) landed **eight commits** that touched `src/` and `tests/` without updating `docs/STATUS.md` and `docs/BENCHMARKS.md` **in the same commit**, so `documentation-checkpoint` failed for that push range on `main`:

`9579f94e`, `ba5ea0cf`, `196ea46f`, `e32c5ed3`, `3bfa1f12`, `34a3efe6`, `2c86f79e`, `f4738bb8`

Each deferred its doc update into a following `record(...)` commit.

## Why it passed locally — the part actually worth fixing

`check-doc-checkpoint.py --staged` inspects the **staged** paths. It is therefore **vacuous when nothing is staged** — which is the normal state after `git commit`, and exactly when `agent-preflight.sh` runs it. The gate reported OK on every one of those commits while checking literally nothing.

CI is **diff-scoped** over the pushed range and checks each commit independently, so the failure only appeared on `main` — where, by that job's own design, a diff-scoped range is never re-covered by a later run.

## The fix

`agent-preflight.sh` now runs `--base origin/main --head HEAD` whenever the branch is ahead of main, reproducing CI's verdict locally in seconds.

That check sits **outside** the `--staged` block, deliberately. My first attempt nested it inside, which reproduces the identical hole one level up: `--staged` is precisely the flag you are *not* passing when the range goes unchecked. Caught by the gate catching my own commit, which is the best evidence it works.

Verified two ways:
- prints `ok doc-checkpoint range` on this branch;
- pointed at the #80 range (`075b9f21..0be5d457`) it raises **20 errors** naming every offending commit.

`workflow.md` carries the same instruction with the reason, so the next series doesn't rediscover it.

## What is *not* being done

**History is not being rewritten.** `main` had already moved (#86 landed on top) and other sessions branch from it, so force-pushing to regroup eight commits' files would cost more than the defect is worth.

**The substance was never wrong.** STATUS, BENCHMARKS and FEATURES on `main` all describe the shipped Vulkan state accurately, with the llvmpipe-only and no-speed-number caveats intact. What was violated is the per-**commit** granularity that keeps a bisect landing on a commit whose docs match its code, and stops a half-landed series from leaving the public surface describing something that doesn't exist.

Recorded in the state log rather than quietly left, since that range stays permanently gate-failed.

## Unrelated pre-existing red

`agent-record` was already failing on `main` at `4cfeee13`, before the #80 merge — `check-fusion-consistency` on `minimax_h3_video_vae_device`. Verified on `origin/main` itself. Not from this work, and not addressed here.

items.title: fix(docs): correct the #82 gate finding — marginal gate, not an N=465 dip
items.body:
Corrects a wrong claim published in #325. Refs #327.

## What was wrong

`docs/benchmarks/i7-12700k.md` stated the N=465 GEMM result was "**reproducible, not measurement noise**" and attributed it to the blocked GEMM's tiling interacting badly with that specific size.

The evidence backing that was invalid in two ways:

1. The three "isolated repeat runs" were taken **on a loaded machine**. native-fast measured 38–40 GFLOP/s there; the same size on an idle machine measures 56.9.
2. Their ratios were compared against **sweep-protocol** ratios rather than like-for-like isolated runs at neighbouring sizes. The control that would have caught this — same protocol, neighbouring sizes, idle machine — was never run. Run since, it gives 82.1% at N=385 and 86.6% at N=545 against 79.5% at N=465, i.e. ordinary variation.

## What the data actually shows

Repeating the identical protocol (same binaries, same sweep, same pinning) on an idle machine fails the gate at a **different set of sizes**:

| N | committed run | verification re-run |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 305 | 80.6% | **78.7%** LOW |
| 385 | 80.2% | **79.0%** LOW |
| 465 | **76.3%** LOW | 82.5% |
| 545 | 80.2% | 86.0% |
| 1025 | 82.1% | **79.2%** LOW |

No size falls below threshold in both runs; per-size spread reaches 6 points. A fine sweep `433:505:8` is flat across the flagged region (58.7 GFLOP/s at N=465, neighbours 58.6–59.5).

**The gate failure is real and reproduces. Only the attribution was wrong.** native-fast averages ~82% of OpenBLAS for N ≥ 256 — inside the epic's 10–20% target — but an 80% threshold applied per-size to a single run has no margin against this variance.

## Changes

- Gate section rewritten around the two-run comparison, with the conclusion stated as a marginal gate rather than a size-specific defect.
- An explicit note recording that the earlier claim was wrong and why, so the correction is visible rather than silently rewritten.
- Caveats strengthened: a **"treat differences under ~5 points as noise"** rule, and the loaded-machine effect (~30% on absolute numbers) as its own bullet.
- Headline bullet reworded from "one reproducible dip" to the marginal-gate framing.
- `benchmarks/README.md` echoed the same claim; fixed there too.

## Verification

`npm run build` — 43 pages, unchanged. No remaining occurrences of the superseded claim.

## Follow-up

#327 tracks the substantive work: reducing measurement variance (`performance` governor, more iterations, report spread) and deciding what the gate should assert, since a per-size single-run threshold at this noise level is a coin flip.

items.title: Make Markdown checks deterministic
items.body:
Closes #32.

## Problem and invariant

The documented broad Markdown glob scanned ignored Rustdoc output, so identical tracked trees produced different results after local builds. Documentation checks must depend only on the reviewed source tree.

## Approach

Pin the Markdownlint configuration and expected tool version, enumerate tracked plus nonignored new Markdown mechanically, exclude ignored/generated paths by construction, repair the tracked baseline, and preserve whitespace checking separately.

## Alternatives rejected

Broad ignores and global rule disables would hide future tracked defects; editing generated Rustdoc would treat disposable output as source.

## Failure modes

Generated files could leak into the corpus, tool versions could drift, or a new tracked document could escape validation. The checker refuses those states and tests a generated-file canary.

## Tests

28 source Markdown files, 0 errors before and after `cargo doc`; ignored-file canary; wrong/missing-version refusal; `git diff --check`.

## Benchmark impact

No runtime impact; documentation lint remains a small repository scan.

## Compatibility and recovery

No API, format, identity, durability, or recovery changes. Reverting restores the former documentation policy.

## Security implications

No permissions, credentials, network access, or executable production surface added.

items.title: Catch docs up to the last three sessions
items.body:
Documentation only. No code changes.

Three sessions of work landed without the docs catching up, and some of what they said had become actively wrong rather than merely incomplete.

## What was stale

**Mutation.** The README, roadmap, and architecture guide all described mutation as limited to pre-built slope and bank sequences, with steep pieces defined in the segment data but unreachable. a011c59 replaced that with validator-driven insertion. I confirmed all six steep IDs (0x05, 0x07, 0x08, 0x0B, 0x0D, 0x0E) appear across 200 random generations. Issue #2 is now closed with that verification.

**Reproducibility.** `docs/architecture.md` listed "Evolution uses the global `random` module with no seed, so runs are not reproducible" as a current limitation. That was fixed in 3755940 back in July.

**The track renderer.** The roadmap described a top-down tile renderer with per-run fitness curves in the present tense, as though it existed. It does not; issue #3 is still open. Rewritten as planned work.

**Test count.** 119 to 158.

**Physics.** `physics.py` was missing from both module listings, and the README said fitness "does not yet reproduce the game's ride-rating calculations" without mentioning that `PhysicsFitness` produces approximate ones. The important qualifier is that its weights are uncalibrated, so that is what the text now says.

**Status table.** The GA-versus-random benchmark was listed as Next; it finished on July 12. Added rows for validator-driven mutation, the physics model, and the buildable-versus-runnable split, and made calibration against headless OpenRCT2 the new Next.

## Devlog

Two new entries covering what had gone unrecorded.

**2026-07-26** on `benchmark_fitness.py`. It was built to answer whether the physics fitness searches differently from the proxy, and instead found that proxy-evolved tracks completed their circuit 10% of the time while passing construction validation 100% of the time.

**2026-08-01** on the two fitness fixes that merged today: separating completability from buildability (#15) and giving `WeightedProxyFitness` the construction penalties it advertised (#16). Includes the thin-margin caveat on the stall screen, the 0.061 height units the real Mine Train clears it by, and why the `create_simple_circuit()` seed made the obvious fix wrong.

## The benchmark re-run

`benchmark_fitness.py`'s committed conclusions predated the stall penalty, so I re-ran it at the same settings. The headline flipped:

| Metric | Proxy (before) | Proxy (now) | Physics |
|---|---|---|---|
| Completes circuit | 10% | 100% | 100% |
| Max speed (m/s) | 2.6 | 7.2 | 8.6 |
| Drops | 0.0 | 0.3 | 0.8 |
| Elevation changes | 4.4 | 7.3 | 11.2 |

The original finding, that physics-evolved tracks beat proxy-evolved tracks on the proxy's own metric, is gone. Each fitness now wins on its own scale: 123.5 against 91.8 under the proxy, 50.6 against 45.7 under physics. That earlier result was a symptom of the stall bug, not a property of the physics fitness.

The script itself is unchanged; only the devlog records the new numbers.

Filed #17 for the `missing_lift_penalty` dead branch found while writing the parity tests, and noted it in the architecture limitations list.

items.body:
Continuation of the codex agent's audit work (its session hit a usage limit mid-flight; picked up per user request). Contains codex's 8 commits on this branch since #17 merged, plus one review-fix commit.

### Codex's commits (reviewed)
- Per-client token-bucket rate limiting (replaces fixed windows; bounded, pruneable)
- Trusted-proxy client identity: `X-Forwarded-For` honored only from an explicit `--trusted-proxy` allow-list
- Predictive KV-memory admission: estimate a request's KV footprint before prefill, reject 503 when it can't fit
- Model-context preflight: reject prompt+completion beyond the model's context window
- Bounded stop-sequence matcher (O(suffix) instead of O(generation²))
- NaN/inf/bool numeric validation; explicit `max_tokens=0` rejected
- Wall-clock cache ages for CLI reporting (was monotonic-mixed, wrong ages)
- Benchmark fingerprinting + comparable-artifact regression gate; nominal-thermal gate for real benchmarks
- Ruff lint gate in CI/release; release checksums + locked dependency manifest; manual real-model verification workflow

### Review fix (the +1 commit)
Both headline guards were **dead code on real models**: they read `model.config`, but mlx-lm models expose `model.args`, and Qwen3.5 nests fields in `text_config`. Discovery now handles both, and the KV estimator is hybrid-aware — it counts only full-attention layers (`layer_types` / `full_attention_interval`), so Qwen3.5 reserves for 8 GQA layers rather than all 32 (the old math would have over-reserved ~4× once activated, spuriously rejecting long prompts). items.title: Record how to benchmark this package, after getting it wrong
items.body:
A 1.53x speedup claim in #170 turned out to be **1.02x**. The cause was measurement, not the change. These are the corrections, written down so they are not rediscovered.

## The workload is serial — measure on one core

25 repeats of an **identical** coupled spectral solve:

| regime | min | CV | max/min |
|---|---|---|---|
| default (128 cores) | 1.718 s | 19.9% | 1.54 |
| 8 cores | 1.706 s | 19.6% | 1.67 |
| 4 cores | 1.696 s | 19.0% | 1.55 |
| **1 core** | **1.692 s** | **3.3%** | **1.11** |

One core is both the **least noisy and the fastest**. The matrices are 25x25 and 78x78 — far too small for XLA's thread pool, which contributes synchronisation overhead and variance and no speedup.

**On the default regime the noise floor (1.54x) exceeds most effects worth measuring.** Every wall-clock comparison I made before establishing this was uninterpretable.

## Consequences for real use

- benchmark under `taskset -c 0`, which resolves effects to a few percent
- run campaigns as independent processes across cores (`workers > 1`), **not** `vmap` — which measured 1.8–2.5x *worse* per point on the implicit path
- report `min` over repeats; it was stable to 1.5% where the mean moved 20%

## Paired interleaving, not sequential blocks

Compiling both arms up front and alternating took the halvings comparison from "1.53x" (single sample, noisy regime) to **1.020x, range 1.008–1.022, unanimous over 12 pairs**.

## A component microbenchmark does not predict the system

The wall root-find is 75% of the coupled RHS op count, and cutting it drops one jitted RHS call from 105.6 µs to 62.5 µs — a real 1.7x. The end-to-end solve moves **2%**.

So the chain `RHS -> jacfwd is 5.4x RHS -> per-iteration cost` does **not** predict end-to-end behaviour, and I used it to justify a number that was off by 25x. Measure the system.

Documentation only — no code change.

items.title: Add the initial requirements catalog
items.body:
Fills `requirements/`, which had existed as an empty, untracked directory since the original scaffold
and was the one directory neither repository-layout table mentioned. Twenty-three architecture-level
security expectations across eleven category files, plus a manifest, a README, and a test.

The catalog is a Stage 3 deliverable and the project is inside Stage 1. That inversion is deliberate:
`future-features.md` lists drafting the initial requirements catalog as priority four of seven, ahead
of context extraction. It adds no product code — `src/` is untouched.

## Where the requirements come from

Provenance turned on a change to OWASP ASVS recent enough to be easy to miss.

ASVS 4.0 had a chapter called "Architecture, Design and Threat Modeling", which is the obvious place
to look. **In ASVS 5.0 that chapter was deleted, not renamed.** Part was dropped as out of scope, the
rest redistributed into domain chapters, and every identifier changed; only eleven of 286 requirements
survived unchanged. Any architecture mapping built on ASVS V1 now points at nothing.

What replaced it is more useful. Every domain chapter in 5.0 opens with an explicit `X.1 Documentation`
section — roughly forty requirements phrased as expectations about what the documentation states rather
than what a running application does. That is a corpus assessable from design documents by
construction, which is what this project consumes. It also pairs: a chapter documents an expectation in
`X.1` and implements it later, the same split as DocumentationGap versus Finding.

| Source | Role |
|---|---|
| OWASP ASVS 5.0.0 | Primary |
| NIST SP 800-53 Release 5.2.0 | Secondary, for ground ASVS puts out of scope: segmentation, availability, retention, external system services |
| OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 | The AI-provider surface neither of the above addresses |

Requirement text is written originally. ASVS is CC BY-SA 4.0, so reproducing its wording would place
the catalog under a share-alike obligation; citing identifiers avoids it and independently satisfies
the clean-room principle in `design-principles.md`.

## What was deliberately excluded

This mattered more than what was included. Three plausible sources are wrong here:

- **CIS Benchmarks.** Every recommendation is an audit procedure against a live account. A document
  asserting MFA is enabled on the root user is a claim, not evidence. Scoring it satisfied would
  manufacture assurance.
- **OWASP SAMM.** It measures organizational process maturity, not a system's design. Asking a maturity
  question of one system's documentation produces precisely the DEC-009 failure.
- **Procedural control families** — NIST `AC-2`, `RA-5`, `CM-3/6/8`, `SI-2/3/4`, the whole `IR` family,
  and CIS's inventory safeguards. A design document's silence on these is normal.

The rule that fell out: a source is usable only where the absence of a control from a design document
is genuine evidence about the design. Where absence is merely normal, the source measures something
else.

## Decisions recorded

- **DEC-010** — store the catalog as version-controlled YAML, one file per primary category, under a
  directory named for the catalog version. `content_hash` is deliberately omitted; it is derived, there
  is no loader to compute or verify it, and a hand-maintained hash is stale after the first edit.
- **DEC-011** — add `common_false_positives` to the Requirement object. DEC-009 says missing
  documentation is not proof of absence, but nothing in the schema recorded *which* wrong conclusion a
  requirement invites. `non_applicable_conditions` says the requirement does not apply;
  `common_false_positives` says what not to conclude when it does apply and the documentation is silent.

## Verification

`tests/unit/test_requirements_catalog.py` runs under a bare `uv run pytest` and enforces schema
conformance against data-model section 17, identifier convention, manifest agreement, and citation
format. It was mutation-tested rather than trusted green: manifest drift, an unknown field, an invalid
severity, and an unversioned citation each fail with the offending requirement named.

The substantive check is against the demo fixtures:

- All four testable intentional non-findings are suppressed by a field that names them, not by
  accident — missing password policy, undescribed database encryption, absent application-managed MFA,
  and absent custom cryptography.
- All five genuine weaknesses remain reachable, each with at least one requirement that would apply.
- The webhook ambiguity resolves the right way: `req-WEBHOOK-001` records "documentation stating only
  that requests are validated, where the mechanism is unstated" as a false positive, so the fixture
  produces a question rather than a finding.
- Non-finding 14.4, that Redis is not internet accessible, is covered by `req-NET-001`. That
  requirement also exposed a limit of ASVS: it scopes itself to the application rather than to where
  the application sits, so it has no boundary-protection requirement at all and `SC-7` carries that
  half alone.

`pyyaml` and `types-pyyaml` are declared as dev dependencies. PyYAML was already present transitively;
declaring it stops the test depending on another package's dependency.

## Known limits

- **Nothing verifies that a cited control identifier exists.** The test checks citation format, not
  existence. Every identifier in 0.1 was verified by hand against the published catalogs, which is a
  guarantee about today rather than about the next edit. Closing it would mean vendoring NIST and ASVS.
- **`req-WEBHOOK-002` carries no ASVS citation.** ASVS 5.0 addresses replay only for authentication
  tokens and has no general inbound-event replay requirement.
- **Severity distribution is uncalibrated**: nine high, thirteen medium, one low, assigned by judgment.
- **The catalog has never been applied to anything.** Every claim about its usefulness is a claim about
  fixtures, not behavior, until the mapping step exists.

items.title: Multicore: fix silenced worker builds, retract hollow claims
items.body:
The most important finding of the release hardening, in three parts.

## The defect that invalidated the telemetry

interceptUpdate returns true at submit; vanilla's updateRenderers then clears needsUpdate on the client; the worker later runs the vanilla body whose head is `if (needsUpdate)` - false by then, so every worker build no-oped and replay swapped empty display lists. Every healthy-looking multicore counter measured hollow swaps. Found by the first framebuffer capture of a multicore scene: empty sky, floating entities, no terrain.

## The fix, verified by pixels

The worker-entry branch restores the flag before the body's check (the body re-clears it itself). Verified: the quiet-world perpetual rebuild loop (~4k hollow rebuilds/min) is gone, capture drain gates open with workers on, and captures now show geometry. A new emptyReplays counter makes hollow builds visible forever.

## The honest consequence

The geometry is WRONG: replayed sections render fragments (docs/benchmarks/multicore-replay-fragments.png - committed as the regression baseline). So this PR also retracts the throughput claim in BENCHMARKS.md, corrects the FEATURES.md row, and records the full account in docs/benchmarks/multicore-status.md, including the institutional lesson: activity counters cannot gate a renderer - output evidence or no claim. Multicore remains default-off and now explicitly marked do-not-enable.

65/65 tests green. rc1 as shipped is safe (feature is opt-in), but its multicore documentation was overstated; this PR is the correction.

Closes #8910

`get_agent_inventory` accepted only `agent_id`, `agent_name`, `kind`, and `limit` — there was no way to filter the returned rows. items.title: Check triage rights with the built-in token
items.body:
# Short description of the changes:
The benchmark trigger's permission gate authenticated with the wrong token and rejected every pull request, including those labelled by admins. Authenticate with the built-in token instead.

# Long description of the changes:
Labelling a pull request with `run-benchmarks` failed at the first step:

```
jglaser has '{"message":"Resource not accessible by personal access token", ... }none' on neutrons/subhkl
Error: jglaser lacks triage rights; refusing to benchmark this pull request.
```

Two things are wrong.

**The token cannot see this repository.** The check ran as `BENCHMARK_DISPATCH_TOKEN`, a fine-grained PAT scoped to `jglaser/subhkl-benchmarks`. Fine-grained tokens reach only their selected repositories, so it holds no permission here at all — not even the `Metadata: read` that `GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/collaborators/{username}/permission` requires. That this repository is public makes no difference. The call returned 403 for every actor, so the gate failed closed on every pull request.

The fix is `${{ github.token }}`. The check asks about a collaborator on the repository the workflow is already running in, so nothing cross-repository is involved. I confirmed against the same endpoint that the built-in token retains `Metadata: read` under `permissions: {}` and returns the expected `admin`, so the empty permissions block stays as it is. The dispatch step keeps the PAT — that step does need to reach another repository.

**A denied lookup did not produce a clean denial.** `gh api` writes the error body to stdout, and the fallback sat inside the command substitution, so `$level` became the whole JSON error with `none` appended rather than `none`. `2>/dev/null` only suppressed the wrapper message. Moving `|| level=none` outside the substitution makes a failed lookup match the deny arm as intended.

Both gates described in #21 are unchanged: the workflow still fires only on `labeled`, and the re-check of triage rights still stands.

items.title: System issuance names scopes outright; the benchmark is documented where it runs
items.body:
Round 1 of the review on [#260](https://github.com/pedrobzz/AckerDB/pull/260) (the 0.17.0 promotion). Two findings, both applied here so the release PR picks them up.

## System issuance could store a grant that widens later

The child invariant is enforced at both ends — subset at issuance, intersection at use — and `systemCredentials` honored only the second. `create` under a parent accepted any pattern, so `orders.*` stored against an identity holding `orders.read` looked correctly narrow and would begin authorizing `orders.write` the day that identity gained it, with nobody having granted the difference. Use-time intersection hides this precisely until it stops being true.

No escalation was ever possible — the intersection holds at every moment — so this is dormancy, not a bypass. But `child-credentials.ts` states the invariant holds at *both* ends, and one door did not.

System authority has no grant of its own to be bounded against, so issuance cannot be checked there the way `credentials.*` checks it. What can be held is the property the invariant exists for: **a concrete grant's expansion is fixed the moment it is stored**, so the scopes an operator names are the most that child can ever reach. Open-ended patterns under a parent now belong to the bounded door. A root credential has no parent to outgrow and keeps its patterns — tested both ways.

## The benchmark was documented in the wrong place

`docs/releases.md` is the authoritative procedure and still said `Fast CI` runs the benchmark and that a promotion is a no-op. That stopped being true when the promotion gate landed. Left alone, an agent reading it would restore the old shape believing the new one was the mistake — the same staleness trap this repo has been deliberate about avoiding. Both it and AGENTS.md now record where the check runs, why the promotion is the right place to measure (the comparison is the whole release delta, not one pull request's slice), and that it is required on `main`.

## Reviewed and left alone

**MCP tool-entry access is not a second authorization model.** `mcp/tool-access.ts` reuses `normalizeScopeRequirement` and `isScopeAuthorized` — the same primitives the function funnel uses — and adds `public`/`authenticated` handling for tool *entries*, which is a curation filter layered on top of the function's own `compileAccess`, not a replacement for it. Its one divergence, that system does not bypass a scoped tool entry, is deliberate and commented. Collapsing it into `compileAccess` would thread that exception through the general funnel to delete three lines: rearranging complexity, not removing it.

**The benchmark's placement itself stands.** It is the owner's decision, and branch protection on `main` already requires `[Release policy, Fast CI, Benchmark]`. Only the documentation was wrong.

items.title: fix(CommandPalette): weigh the grapheme-snap ceiling against the value
items.body:
### Linked issue

Closes #387.

### Type of change

- [ ] Documentation (updates to the documentation or readme)
- [x] Bug fix (a non-breaking change that fixes an issue)
- [ ] Enhancement (improving an existing functionality)
- [ ] New feature (a non-breaking change that adds functionality)
- [ ] Chore (updates to the build process or auxiliary tools and libraries)
- [ ] Breaking change (fix or feature that would cause existing functionality to change)

### Description

`GRAPHEME_SNAP_MAX_LENGTH` is documented, and was tested, as a bound on the field text. It was not measured against it. `truncateHTMLFromStart` built its snapper from `content` — the value *after* escaping and *after* mark insertion — so the ceiling was reached early, by an amount nothing in the constant hints at. Escaping has no fixed overhead: `&` expands to five characters, `"` to six.

```js
const FLAG = '\u{1F1FA}\u{1F1F8}'   // 🇺🇸

'a'.repeat(8140) + FLAG.repeat(10) + 'match'     // value.length 8185 — under the ceiling
'&'.repeat(1600) + FLAG.repeat(50) + 'match'     // value.length 1805 — 22% of the ceiling
```

Both degraded, and both rendered 🇸🇺 with an orphaned regional indicator where the author wrote 🇺🇸 — a **different country**, with nothing to signal the loss. That is the defect #364 describes and #371 exists to prevent, reappearing above a threshold no reader could predict from the constant.

### Fix

`createClusterSnapper` takes the length to weigh separately from the string to segment, named `fieldTextLength` for what it is. The parameter is **required**, not defaulted to `value.length`: a default is precisely what would let the next derived-string caller inherit this bug in silence.

### Cost

Segmenting a string the ceiling would have excluded is affordable — but not because the call is cheap in isolation. On a long run of regional indicators it is not, since `containing()` walks the run. It is that `Array.from(html)` above it already paid the larger price on the same string, unconditionally, on both sides of this fix.

Measured end to end, this branch against the old behaviour on identical input:

| input | old | new | delta |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| plain, `value.length` 8185 | 86 µs → 🇸🇺 | 98 µs → 🇺🇸 | +11 µs |
| escape-heavy, `value.length` 1505 | 172 µs → 🇺🇸 | 167 µs → 🇺🇸 | −6 µs |

Within noise in both directions. An independent A/B through `vitest bench` (400+ samples, ~2% RME) reached the same conclusion: 1.1879 ms vs 1.1843 ms on the all-quotes worst case at the ceiling.

`test/bench/search.bench.ts` gains `under the ceiling, escaped six-fold`, which reaches the ceiling by escaping rather than by length, so the claim rests on a durable measurement rather than a throwaway script — the convention that file's own header sets.

**An earlier revision of this description carried a cost table that was wrong by three orders of magnitude.** The benchmark behind it built the `Segments` view once and reused it across iterations, while the real code builds a fresh view per truncation. Recording that here because the number was quoted in the commit message and the source comment too, and the comment now explains the trap instead of restating a figure.

### Tests

The two ceiling tests moved off `value.length + MARKUP` onto `value.length`. That makes `snaps clusters exactly at the ceiling` the plain-text repro in its own right — a value of exactly the advertised length previously degraded, verified against `main`.

`measures the ceiling against the value, not its escaped copy` covers the unbounded half. It was missing because no fixture in `degraded paths` contained an escapable character, so only the fixed 13-character single-mark overhead was ever exercised.

Mutation-checked: reverting the segmenter gate to the derived string, passing `content.length` at the call site, moving `GRAPHEME_SNAP_MAX_LENGTH` by ±1, and ignoring the new parameter are each caught by a named test.

732 tests green (`test/utils/`, `test/components/`); `eslint` and `vue-tsc --noEmit` clean. `test/utils/search.spec.ts` run 38 consecutive times on a quiet tree, all green — two reviewers reported intermittent failures in these tests, which reproduced only while a concurrent mutation-testing pass had the file modified, and whose failure signature matches that mutation exactly.

### Documentation

`.sync/PORTING.md`'s guard entry said the threshold *"is crossed 13 characters earlier than a reading of `value.length` suggests"*. That described the defect rather than the design, so it is corrected here rather than deferred to the documentation follow-up — a porter reading the old sentence could have restored the bug deliberately.

### Provenance

The defect was found by an independent review pass over #371 — five reviewers reading the merged code, rather than the authoring session re-reading itself. #371's own description argued its three self-review rounds were not converging; this is what that looked like in practice. The wrong cost figure, the parameter name, the missing default, and the deferred documentation fix were all caught by a second such pass over this branch.

### Checklist

- [x] I have linked an issue or discussion.
- [x] I have updated the documentation accordingly.

items.title: ci: exempt test_bench_execute_decim_64k from the perf gate
items.body:
The advisory perf gate has failed on two PRs containing **no DSP code whatsoever** — #519 (docs only, +59.7%) and #524 (build tooling only, +66.5%). A gate that fires on documentation changes stops being read, so it's worth establishing what it's actually measuring.

## It isn't jitter, and it isn't the runner

Both measurement phases were internally *tight* — ~1.2% stddev each — and simply disagreed with each other. And in the same CI run, two large FIR benchmarks agreed across those same two phases to within 0.15%:

| benchmark | base min | head min | Δ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `bench_fir::test_bench_execute[409600]` | 19,135,333 ns | 19,107,997 ns | **−0.14%** |
| `bench_fir::test_bench_execute[819200]` | 38,290,100 ns | 38,288,683 ns | **−0.004%** |
| `bench_Resampler::test_bench_execute_decim_64k` | 1,104,593 ns | 1,839,419 ns | **+66.5%** |

So the runner was neither throttled nor systematically biased against the head — which were my first two hypotheses, and both are wrong. The C benchmark shifted identically (58.44 → 35.12 MSa/s), so it isn't a Python-layer artifact either.

What's left is a benchmark that lands in one of **two internally-stable states ~1.66× apart**, fixed per process. That's the signature of memory layout — allocation alignment or hugepage backing — not of code.

## Why exempt rather than fix

It doesn't reproduce here: **448 µs ± 0.2% across 8 separate processes** on the reference machine. Without a local repro, any change to the benchmark would be a guess dressed as a fix, and would also break comparability with the published v0.10.1→v0.37.3 history.

Note that jm already compares the **`min`** sample rather than the mean, precisely because means are noisy on shared runners (`_bench.py::_bench_metric`) — and it still fires, because bimodality moves the floor itself. No choice of statistic rescues this one.

## The change

One line, via jm's own mechanism (`bench --check --allow`): still measured, still reported with its delta, just unable to fail the build. The list sits in the Makefile next to `BENCH_THRESHOLD` — the Makefile is the single driver for the gate (#524) — and the comment requires each entry to justify why the *measurement*, not the code, is untrustworthy. Exemptions are blind spots; this one is worth it, a permanently-ignored gate is not.

Verified against jm's comparator with the real CI numbers:

```
allow=no  -> status=regressed  delta=66.5%
allow=yes -> status=allowed    delta=66.5%
```

items.title: research: the operating-point invariant is already enforced
items.body:
Corrects a claim I merged one turn earlier in #142. One documentation file, read-only investigation.

## What was wrong

The note said a DB-side `CHECK`/trigger was **owed** to make the invariant structural, and deferred applying it because the database was under continuous concurrent write.

Probing showed **both halves were wrong.**

## 1. The invariant is already enforced

`world_benchmark_operating_point` is a **VIEW, not a base table**, and its body ends:

```sql
  FROM world_benchmark_meta m
    JOIN world_benchmark_aggregate a ON a.meta_id = m.id
    LEFT JOIN world_benchmark_timing_aggregate t
      ON t.meta_id = a.meta_id AND t.scope = a.scope AND t.archiver = a.archiver
 WHERE m.task = 'CUBR-0087-phaseC' AND a.archiver = 'cubrim';
```

`a.archiver = 'cubrim'` is hardcoded in the view body. **I1 and I2 cannot be violated** — the view cannot emit a non-cubrim row, and no constraint could be attached to it in any case, because a view has no rows of its own to constrain. The `competitor_note` documents a property the SQL already guarantees rather than a convention a reader must uphold.

The timing join is equally tight: it matches on `meta_id`, `scope` **and** `archiver`, so speed columns on any row come from that row's own meta. No cross-meta value can enter the view through the join either.

## 2. The deferral reason was overstated

Probed directly rather than inferred from PR activity: **one active backend** (this session's own query) and **zero locks** on the target relation. The database was quiet, not busy.

## What actually remains

**I3 — and no constraint can fix it.** A comparison that spans `meta_id` is a property of how a *reader* queries `world_benchmark_timing_aggregate`; the mistake happens in the query, not in stored data. The defence is the measurement already in the note: metas 37 and 38 carry a single archiver, so a competitor comparison at those operating points **does not exist to be read**.

Nothing is owed against this view.

## Why this matters enough to correct

Leaving "enforcement owed" on `main` would have sent a future session to write a redundant constraint on an object that cannot hold one — burning time and probably ending in confusion about why `ALTER VIEW ... ADD CHECK` fails.

The decision itself is unchanged and still stands: comparisons come from the timing aggregate, only within a single `meta_id`.

Read-only throughout — no database object created, altered, or dropped; `evaluation` remains 0.

CI note: `ci.yml` path filters exclude `documentation/**`, so `ci.yml` is dispatched manually on this branch head.

items.title: docs: stop publishing performance numbers nobody measured
items.body: Companion cleanup for #196. ## The problem `benchmarks.md` published latency, throughput and resource tables that nobody ever ran: `<5ms` overhead, `p95 35ms`, `700 qps` at four instances, `300` audit writes/sec. They were reasoned from what the architecture *ought* to cost, labelled "target" once at the top of the page — and then quoted in `comparison.md` with the qualifier stripped off, where they read as measured facts about a shipped product. For a project whose pitch is auditability, an invented number is a worse liability than a missing one. The first prospect who measures us discredits the exact attribute we sell. ## What changed **`benchmarks.md`** — 350 lines of fabricated tables → a stub that says plainly nothing is measured, states the one thing we *can* say without measuring (the audit write is synchronous and on the critical path by design, so it can't be optimised out of a benchmark without measuring a gateway we don't ship), explains why we're waiting for a quiet machine rather than publishing shared-VPS numbers, and commits to publishing bad results too. **`comparison.md`** — kept in full; it's the stronger page and needs no benchmarks. Removed only the unmeasured parts (~44 lines touched of 362): | Removed | Replaced with | |---|---| | `<5ms` / `+5ms` overhead, 4 sites | "Not measured", linked to benchmarks.md | | TCO day-estimates + "Break-Even Point: 4-6 months" | A table of what you'd have to rebuild in a custom wrapper — the honest form of that argument | | "Effort Estimate: 1-2 days" | A statement that we have no sample to estimate from | | "Production-optimized", "Battle-tested" | "Not measured", "Typed errors with stable codes" | | PgBouncer `<1ms` vs `+5ms` row | Work-per-query: pool checkout vs authz + SQL guard + synchronous audit write | ## Verification `npm run build` in `website/` passes; all new relative links resolve. The two broken-anchor warnings it reports (`auth-sso#state--persistence`, `roadmap#mysql--mssql-deferred`) are pre-existing in files this PR doesn't touch.
